examInfo: Exam 3: 35 multiple-choice questions on new material only: Dr. Taylor's Lecture A and L17-L22. Nothing from Exam 1 or Exam 2's lectures.
Friday, November 20, 8:00-9:30 am (the dental students' sitting; optometry sits at 10:00).
In person, Volker Hall Lecture Room B, on Canvas with LockDown Browser, as for Exams 1 and 2.

A Dental endocrinology clinical application (Dr. Taylor), L17 Pregnancy and lactation (Dr. Madison), L18 Estrogens and androgens (Dr. Fasinu), L19 Introduction to hematology (Dr. Herr), L20 Lymphomas and leukemias (Dr. Borak), L21 and L22 Pathology of the male and female reproductive systems (Dr. Dal Zotto).
Dr. Taylor's lecture was taught November 6 but left off Exam 2 (Dr. Herr said he forgot it), so it moved to Exam 3 with everything the Exam 2 hub had for it.

L19 and L20 are taught Tuesday, November 17, and their notes here come from the slides until the recordings are posted. L21 and L22 are Wednesday, November 18, and join this hub when their slides are posted.
The count per lecture hasn't been announced. The mock gives each lecture 5, one for each hour of class.
Quiz 4 is due Thursday, November 19, at 11:59 pm. This hub uses nothing from the quizzes or the take-home.

likelyTopics.t: Hypoglycemia in the chair: the signs, a finger-stick (some CGMs stop reading at a floor), straight glucose rather than table sugar, a slow response on a GLP-1 drug, glucagon IM or subcutaneously if oral glucose fails

Before treating a diabetic: HbA1c above 7 is poorly controlled (implant failure, periodontal disease), confirm the meal and medication, morning appointments; Dr. Taylor's metformin with a skipped breakfast; pack-years
Hyperthyroidism and Graves disease (his first case): epinephrine caution, and thyroid storm (fever, pulse 140 or more; call 911)
Addison disease (his third case): oral pigment from high ACTH, adrenal crisis triggers and signs, extra corticosteroid after a big procedure; Cushing syndrome and long-term steroids
Hyperparathyroidism on the radiograph (lost lamina dura, radiolucent brown tumors, mobility) and the calcium regulators (PTH, vitamin D, calcitonin)
Acromegaly's growing jaw (Class I to Class III, diastemas, macroglossia); growth plates fused by the sex hormones, and implant timing
The three hormone classes with examples, receptors, and endocrine versus nervous signaling
Diabetes: type 1 versus type 2 (insulin ineffective, not deficient), oral manifestations and the sugar in saliva, the two-way periodontal link, SGLT2 drugs and UTIs
Hyperthyroid versus hypothyroid dental considerations (hypothyroidism far more common), and the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery
Sex hormones and the mouth: puberty, pregnancy gingivitis and the interproximal pyogenic granuloma, menopause
Pituitary hormones (ADH and diabetes insipidus), alpha and beta cells, and the adrenal medulla

hCG rescues the corpus luteum: made by the trophoblasts, it keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone and estrogen through the first trimester, LH and FSH stay suppressed, and it is what a pregnancy test measures
Prolactin makes the milk and oxytocin lets it down through the myoepithelial cells; during pregnancy progesterone antagonizes prolactin, so full milk production waits for delivery
Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin; suckling lowers dopamine and raises oxytocin from the posterior pituitary; prolactin inhibits GnRH, so periods stop
Fertilization: ZP3 sets off the acrosomal reaction, the sperm then binds ZP2, the oocyte finishes its second meiotic division, and the cortical reaction blocks polyspermy

The pregnancy steroids: estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy; the placenta makes progesterone on its own but needs the fetal adrenal's 17,20 desmolase and the fetal liver before its aromatase makes estriol

Labor: the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio rises; uterine distention, prostaglandins (PGF2 alpha for contraction, PGE2 for the cervix) and oxytocin from the posterior pituitary; oxytocin limits bleeding after delivery
The placenta's other hormones: human placental lactogen opposes insulin (an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic pregnancy and gestational diabetes); relaxin keeps the uterus quiet
Implantation at the blastocyst stage: trophoblasts, cytotrophoblasts (nurse cells) versus syncytiotrophoblasts (invasion), and decidualization
Capacitation: why ejaculated sperm can't fertilize yet, and the membrane changes that make the acrosomal reaction possible
Maternal hormones that promote fertilization: estrogen at ovulation helps the sperm, then holds the embryo back until progesterone relaxes the myometrium
The endocrine basis of contraception: the pill blunts the LH surge, progestin thickens the cervical mucus, high-dose estrogen prevents implantation

Thromboembolism, the estrogens' most serious side effect: more clotting factors and less antithrombin III; shared by the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors (his raloxifene dental case); oral anticoagulants work less well; any clot, even years ago, rules estrogen out
Testosterone's two fates: 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT, the active form, and aromatase makes estradiol (the tall, osteoporotic man without aromatase); DHEA, the over-the-counter precursor

The anti-androgens: why a long-acting GnRH analog (goserelin) switches testosterone off; finasteride and dutasteride (Proscar versus Propecia, his finasteride dental case); the receptor antagonists flutamide and bicalutamide
SERMs: why they are selective; tamoxifen (breast antagonist, uterine agonist, ER-positive tumors only), raloxifene for osteoporosis, clomiphene for ovulation

Testosterone's adverse effects and cautions: hepatotoxicity (the most important), virilization in women, feminization in men, the gel at bedtime, and when to avoid it (BPH, pregnancy, breast cancer in men)

Emergency contraception and the progestins: Plan B (levonorgestrel, 72 hours, no prescription) versus ulipristal (an antagonist, 5 days, prescription); progestin-only pills when estrogen is ruled out; levonorgestrel is not estrogenic
Aromatase inhibitors: anastrozole blocks testosterone's conversion to estradiol to treat breast cancer; hot flashes and thromboembolism; not before menopause
The estrogen drugs: estradiol from the ovary, ethinyl estradiol in oral contraceptives, estrone in Premarin for menopause; the indications
How the sex steroids act (nuclear receptors, carried on SHBG) and what testosterone does (red cells, water retention, muscle); testosterone cypionate, the depot

The spleen's white and red pulp: T cells in the PALS around the central arteriole, the marginal zone of macrophages and some B cells, red pulp of splenic cords and sinusoids, no cortex or medulla, and what the spleen does

The thymus: the dense, dark cortex versus the lighter medulla with Hassall's corpuscles, its epithelioreticular stroma, the three layers of the blood-thymus barrier, and involution to fat from the early teens

T cell education: precursors in through postcapillary venules, positive selection in the cortex, negative selection in the medulla, single CD4 or CD8 cells out, and 95 to 99 percent dying by apoptosis
Blood through the spleen: sheathed capillaries emptying into the splenic cords (the open circulation), and the slit-walled sinuses the cells squeeze back into
Where B and T cells sit: lymph node cortex follicles (B) versus paracortex (T), MALT nodules (B) and the areas around them (T), and blood lymphocytes entering a node through high endothelial venules

Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs: the bone marrow and thymus make B and T cells immunocompetent without antigen (B and NK cells mature in the marrow, T cells in the thymus); lymph nodes, MALT and the spleen activate them

Telling the white cells apart by their features and jobs: the neutrophil (multi-lobed, bacteria), eosinophil (red granules, parasites and allergy), basophil (dark blue granules, heparin, asthma) and monocyte (becomes the macrophage)
The lymphocyte classes: B cells (surface IgM and IgD), helper T cells (CD4, MHC II), cytotoxic T cells (CD8, perforins, allograft rejection) and NK cells (CD16 binding IgG in ADCC)
Innate versus adaptive immunity: pre-existing barriers, low pH, lysozyme, thiocyanate in saliva, phagocytes and NK cells, versus antibodies (humoral) and T cells (cellular)
MALT and the tonsils: M cells carrying antigen into the Peyer's patches, IgA into the lumen, and adenoiditis of the pharyngeal tonsil
AML's diagnostic threshold (20 percent blasts for most AML, any count with a defining genetic abnormality), blasts and Auer rods (which exclude ALL), and AML versus ALL
Acute promyelocytic leukemia: abnormal promyelocytes with Auer rod bundles, t(15;17) PML::RARA, coagulopathy and DIC, ATRA plus arsenic trioxide
Chronic myeloid leukemia: BCR::ABL1 and the Philadelphia chromosome, chronic versus blast phase, a leukocytosis of maturing neutrophils, imatinib
Acute versus chronic leukemia (onset, course, blasts, platelets, organomegaly) and leukemia's two kinds of symptoms, marrow failure and organ infiltration
Burkitt lymphoma: endemic versus sporadic and their EBV rates, t(8;14) and MYC, the starry sky, the jaw
Diagnosing lymphoma: tissue sampling, a fresh specimen (not formalin) for flow cytometry, forward and side scatter, the B symptoms
Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin: Reed-Sternberg cells in a reactive background, contiguous nodes above the diaphragm, a rare extranodal start; 85 to 90 percent of lymphoid neoplasms are B-cell
Follicular lymphoma's t(14;18) and BCL2, mantle cell lymphoma's t(11;14), and the infections behind MALT lymphoma
CLL/SLL: soccer-ball chromatin and smudge cells in the blood; one disease, split by a B-cell count of 5 × 10⁹/L; older patients; largely incurable
Extramedullary AML in the gums (myeloid sarcoma), and B-ALL, the leukemia of young children
Plasma cell neoplasms: plasmacytoma versus multiple myeloma, rouleaux, the M-spike and CRAB
The T-cell lymphomas: Sézary syndrome's triad, and extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma of the nose and palate
